claims.text: Conventionally processed high-entropy alloys typically exhibit trade-offs among strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
Changing thermal-treatment parameters can alter nanoscale structure in medium- or high-entropy alloys.
Heat treatment at 700–900°C with optimized dwell times and rapid quenching under inert conditions will produce a refined hierarchical matrix.
The proposed thermal treatment will produce uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
The resulting refined matrix and nanoscale precipitates will be stable.
Hard nanoscale precipitates will strengthen the alloy and resist deformation.
A softer matrix surrounding the strengthening phase will retain ductility.
A hierarchical hard/soft microstructure can improve strength and plasticity together.
The proposed precipitate/matrix structure will maintain a balanced Young’s modulus.
The proposed hierarchical structure will enhance fracture resistance.

The treatment will simultaneously improve strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance by approximately 10–15%, or by a statistically significant amount, relative to untreated or conventionally treated material.
An inert atmosphere is required to prevent oxidation during the thermal treatment.
The claimed benefits are restricted to the 700–900°C treatment window.
Oxidation, temperatures outside 700–900°C, or compositional segregation may eliminate the proposed microstructural and mechanical benefits.
The magnitude of improvement will vary with alloy composition and processing details.
Other uncontrolled microstructural features may cause variability in the mechanical-property enhancement.
Atom probe tomography can characterize heat-treatment-induced nanoscale chemical ordering, although the cited evidence does not establish its use here for uniformly dispersed precipitates.
